overview.text: The Sicilian Mafia is a network of organized-crime groups rooted in Sicily. Its best-known organization, Cosa Nostra, operates through local families, hierarchy, secrecy, and territorial control. The word “Mafia” has been used for Sicilian criminal groups since the nineteenth century. Extortion, money laundering, and drug trafficking have been among Cosa Nostra’s activities. Sicilian networks built links across the Atlantic, including heroin-smuggling networks exposed in the Pizza Connection investigation. American La Cosa Nostra developed from Sicilian roots but has its own history and structure, so the two should not be treated as a single identical organization. Both are distinct from other Italian criminal groups such as the Camorra.

key_facts.text: Cosa Nostra means “Our Thing.”
The term “Mafia” has been applied to Sicilian criminal groups since the mid-nineteenth century.
Extortion and money laundering are among Sicilian Cosa Nostra activities.
The Pizza Connection case exposed a Sicilian Mafia heroin-smuggling network.
American La Cosa Nostra evolved from, but is distinct from, the Sicilian Mafia.

overview.text: Egypt is a modern country whose mainland lies at the northeastern corner of Africa, while its Sinai Peninsula extends into Asia. The Mediterranean Sea borders it to the north and the Red Sea to the east; Libya and Sudan are its western and southern neighbors. Most of its land is desert, while the Nile Valley and the river’s northern delta contain the main areas of settlement. This geography makes the Nile central to Egypt’s settlement pattern. The Suez Canal crosses Egyptian territory between the Mediterranean and Red seas. It separates the African mainland from Asia and gives ships a direct route between the two seas. The canal runs just west of Sinai, making Egypt a country that spans two continents.

key_facts.text: Egypt lies in northeastern Africa.
Libya borders Egypt on the west and Sudan on the south.
Most Egyptians live in the Nile Valley or Nile Delta.
The Suez Canal links the Mediterranean and Red seas.
The canal separates the African continent from Asia.
Egypt extends into Asia through the Sinai Peninsula.

overview.text: Ancient Egypt was a long-lived civilization centered on the Nile Valley and Delta. Its kings ruled a realm traditionally divided into Upper Egypt in the south and Lower Egypt in the north, even after the two regions became united under the earliest dynasties. Kingship, religion, and burial customs changed over many centuries. During the Old Kingdom, rulers built pyramids as parts of funerary complexes; Djoser’s Step Pyramid at Saqqara and Khufu’s Great Pyramid at Giza are famous examples. Much later, in the New Kingdom, Hatshepsut ruled as a female pharaoh. Monuments and tombs preserve much of what historians know about this civilization.

key_facts.text: Upper Egypt lay south of Lower Egypt, despite their names.
Upper and Lower Egypt were united by the first rulers of Dynasty 1.
Djoser’s Step Pyramid at Saqqara was Egypt’s first pyramid.
Khufu’s Great Pyramid at Giza belongs to the Old Kingdom.
Hatshepsut ruled in Dynasty 18 during the New Kingdom.

overview.text: The Second Defenestration of Prague took place on 23 May 1618 at Prague Castle in Bohemia. Protestant nobles, angry at what they saw as violations of their religious rights by the Catholic Habsburg ruler, confronted imperial officials and threw two governors and a secretary from a window. All three survived. “Defenestration” literally means throwing someone out of a window. The episode sparked the Bohemian Revolt, whose first phase included the Battle of White Mountain in 1620. It is also commonly treated as the opening of the Thirty Years’ War, which spread far beyond Bohemia and drew in many European powers.

overview.text: Operation Desert Storm was the combat campaign that drove Iraqi forces from Kuwait in 1991. Iraq had occupied Kuwait since August 1990, and the United States and partner nations first assembled forces nearby during Operation Desert Shield. Desert Storm opened with coalition air attacks in mid-January. The ground offensive began on 24 February and moved rapidly into Kuwait and southern Iraq; coalition forces liberated Kuwait by 28 February. General Norman Schwarzkopf commanded the coalition forces. The operation was the fighting phase of the larger Gulf War crisis, which had begun months before the air campaign.

overview.text: The Gulf War of 1990–1991 began when Saddam Hussein’s Iraq invaded and occupied neighboring Kuwait on 2 August 1990. The United Nations demanded Iraqi withdrawal and imposed sanctions, while a United States-led coalition assembled forces in the region. After Iraq failed to withdraw, the coalition launched an air campaign in January 1991 and a ground offensive on 24 February. Coalition troops expelled Iraqi forces from Kuwait within days. Disputes over war debts, oil production, and territory had strained relations between Iraq and Kuwait before the invasion. The Gulf War thus spans the invasion, months of diplomacy and military buildup, and the coalition’s 1991 air and ground campaign.

overview.text: The Vichy government governed part of France after the country’s defeat by Germany in 1940. The June armistice divided France into German-occupied and initially unoccupied zones; the new French government established itself in the town of Vichy. Led by Marshal Philippe Pétain, it claimed neutrality but cooperated with Nazi Germany under the armistice and later pursued an openly collaborationist policy. Vichy officials enacted antisemitic laws, seized Jewish property, interned people, and helped round up Jews for deportation. German forces occupied the southern zone as well in 1942. The regime’s history shows that persecution in wartime France involved French administrators as well as German occupiers.

key_facts.text: France signed an armistice with Germany on 22 June 1940.
The armistice initially divided France into occupied and unoccupied zones.
The new government was based in Vichy and led by Philippe Pétain.
Vichy officials enacted antisemitic laws and participated in deportations of Jews.

overview.text: Gaius Marius was a Roman general and politician of the late Republic who held the consulship an unprecedented seven times. Elected consul for the first time in 107 BCE, he led Roman forces in the war against Jugurtha of Numidia and recruited volunteers from poorer citizens. His later armies defeated the Teutones near Aquae Sextiae in 102 BCE and the Cimbri in 101 BCE. Marius’s military reputation brought him repeated elections but also sharpened political rivalries. His former officer Sulla became his most consequential opponent during Rome’s civil conflicts. Marius returned to power with Cinna, won a seventh consulship, and died early in 86 BCE.

key_facts.text: Marius first became consul in 107 BCE.
He recruited poor volunteers for the campaign against Jugurtha.
His army defeated the Teutones near Aquae Sextiae in 102 BCE.
Marius defeated the Cimbri in 101 BCE.

overview.text: The Yellow Turban Rebellion was a major uprising against China’s Eastern Han dynasty in 184 CE. Zhang Jiao, also rendered Zhang Jue, led followers of a religious movement called the Way of Great Peace. Rebels wore yellow head coverings, giving the revolt its name. It arose amid political disorder and wider social conflict late in the Han period. Although the main revolt was suppressed, the crisis exposed the weakening authority of the imperial court and helped create the setting for regional warlords. The Eastern Han finally ended in 220, after which the rival states of Wei, Shu, and Wu formed the Three Kingdoms period.

key_facts.text: The Yellow Turban Uprising began in 184 CE under the Eastern Han.
Zhang Jiao, also called Zhang Jue, led the movement.
The rebels were named for their yellow head coverings.
The movement had religious beliefs associated with the later development of Daoism.
The Eastern Han ended in 220 and gave way to the Three Kingdoms.

overview.text: Idi Amin Dada was a Ugandan military officer who seized power from President Milton Obote in a January 1971 coup and ruled until 1979. His government used violent purges and security forces to suppress opponents. In August 1972 he first ordered Asian holders of British passports to leave Uganda, then broadened the expulsion to other Asians, forcing many to leave homes and businesses. Amin’s invasion of Tanzanian territory helped bring a Tanzanian and Ugandan exile campaign that overthrew him in 1979. He fled into exile and died in 2003. The expulsions disrupted families and businesses, while his violent rule drove many other Ugandans into exile.

key_facts.text: Amin seized power in a January 1971 coup against Milton Obote.
His regime used violent purges against political opponents.
On 4 August 1972, Amin announced that Asian holders of British passports must leave Uganda.
Tanzanian forces and Ugandan exiles overthrew Amin in 1979.
Amin died in exile in 2003.
